entities.summary:
Caius, the 28th Bishop of Rome, served as pontiff from December 17, 283 CE, until his death on April 22, 296 CE, during a pivotal period of the late Roman Empire. Emerging from Dalmatia, possibly Salona, he held the papacy for over twelve years, a tenure marked by both relative peace for Christians under Emperor Carinus and the escalating tensions preceding the Great Persecution under Diocletian. His leadership was critical in consolidating the nascent structure of the Roman Church and navigating its relationship with imperial authority, establishing precedents for future papal roles.

During his pontificate, Caius is traditionally credited with several key ecclesiastical developments, though historical evidence for some remains debated. He is said to have decreed that a bishop must pass through the orders of doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon before consecration, formalizing a hierarchical progression within the clergy. Furthermore, he allegedly stipulated that bishops should be consecrated by three other bishops, reinforcing collegiality and apostolic succession. While these reforms likely evolved over time, their attribution to Caius underscores his perceived role in standardizing ecclesiastical governance. His tenure also saw the continued growth of the Christian community in Rome, despite underlying imperial suspicion.
